lead: A microwave resonator stores electric and magnetic energy and returns it at one frequency, f0. Energy sloshes between a capacitor and an inductor, or in the fields of a cavity or line section. Q, the quality factor, compares energy stored with energy lost per radian. High Q gives a narrow response; low Q gives a broad one. Resonators sit inside filters, oscillators, duplexers and frequency meters — every block that picks one frequency and rejects the rest.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for distributed L and C, 1.3 for the input impedance of shorted and open lines, and 1.7 for waveguide modes.

blocks.text: A series RLC circuit has impedance Z = R + j(ωL − 1/(ωC)), where R is resistance in ohms, L inductance in henries, C capacitance in farads and ω = 2πf the angular frequency in rad/s. At one frequency the reactances cancel: ω0L = 1/(ω0C). The impedance drops to R and current peaks. That is resonance.

blocks.where: f0 is the resonant frequency in hertz, L is inductance in henries, C is capacitance in farads.

blocks.text: A parallel RLC circuit is the dual. At the same f0 its admittance is minimum, so impedance and voltage peak. Both circuits are resonators: they store energy and give it back.

The sharpness of that peak is Q, the quality factor: Q = ω0 × (energy stored) ÷ (power lost). A lossless circuit has infinite Q; a lossy one has a rounded peak. Q also equals f0 divided by the 3 dB bandwidth.

blocks.where: ω0 = 2πf0 in rad/s, W is the energy stored in joules, P<sub>loss</sub> is the power lost in watts.

blocks.text: For a series circuit Q = ω0L/R = (1/R)√(L/C); for a parallel circuit Q = Rp/(ω0L) = ω0RpC, with Rp the shunt resistance in ohms. A large series R spoils Q; a small shunt Rp spoils it. Every resonator is an L–C pair plus one loss resistance.

A real resonator is coupled to a source and a load, so three Q values describe it. Q0, the unloaded Q, counts only internal loss (metal, dielectric, radiation). Qe, the external Q, counts only the power leaving through the coupling. QL, the loaded Q, counts both; they combine like parallel resistors.

blocks.where: QL, Q0 and Qe are dimensionless quality factors: loaded, unloaded and external.
f0 is the resonant frequency in hertz and BW is the 3 dB (half-power) bandwidth in hertz — the width over which the response stays above 1/√2 = 0.707 of its peak.

blocks.text: A QL of 100 at 2 GHz means a 20 MHz bandwidth. After the drive is removed the field amplitude decays as exp(−t/τ) with τ = 2QL/ω0 (the stored energy decays twice as fast). The coupling coefficient g = Q0/Qe says how hard the resonator is coupled: g < 1 is undercoupled, g = 1 critically coupled (QL = Q0/2, all power absorbed at f0), and g > 1 overcoupled.

Below about 1 GHz a resonator is a coil and a capacitor. At 10 GHz the needed L and C are so small that the coil is a fraction of a millimetre and its resistance destroys Q. Microwave design therefore uses distributed resonators, where a line or metal box stores the energy.

λ/2 resonator. A line of length l = λ/2 shorted at its far end shows Zin = 0 at its input at f0: a series resonance. The same length open at the far end shows Zin = ∞: a parallel resonance. Resonance repeats at every multiple of f0.

λ/4 resonator. A shorted stub of length λ/4 shows infinite input impedance at its open end — it behaves as a parallel resonant circuit. A physical short becomes an electrical open. An open λ/4 stub is the dual and shows a series resonance.

blocks.where: c is the speed of light in the filling medium in m/s, a, b, d are the cavity width, height and length in metres, and m, n, p are the mode indices (TEmnp or TMmnp).

blocks.text: A closed metal box is a waveguide with walls at both ends, so only certain field patterns fit: it is a rectangular cavity resonator with these frequencies. Its Q of several thousand comes from the large volume-to-surface ratio, and it falls as the surface resistance Rs = √(πfμ/σ) grows, where f is frequency in hertz, μ the permeability of the metal in H/m and σ its conductivity in S/m. For the TE10p mode of a cavity of width a, height b and length d, Q0 = (kad)³bη / (2π²Rs) × 1/(2p²a³b + 2bd³ + p²a³d + ad³), with k = 2πf0/c and η = 377 Ω.

items: Dielectric resonator: a ceramic puck with εr of a few tens and Q set mainly by its loss tangent, Qd ≈ 1/tan δ, often several thousand. Small enough to sit on a printed board.
Microstrip resonator: a printed λ/2 open line. Q is modest, tens to a few hundred, because the fields touch lossy dielectric and thin metal.

figure.caption: The resonator of worked example 1: QL = 100 gives a 20 MHz band at 2 GHz. Loosened to critical coupling (Qe = Q0 = 500) the same resonator has QL = 250 and an 8 MHz band.

spec.aria: Two resonance curves centred on 2 gigahertz, a wider one for loaded Q 100 with its 20 megahertz half-power band marked, and a narrower dashed one for loaded Q 250.

examples.question: A bandpass resonator is centred at f0 = 2 GHz. Its 3 dB bandwidth measured on a network analyser is 20 MHz. (a) Find the loaded Q. (b) The unloaded Q of the resonator alone is 500. Find the external Q and comment on the coupling.
steps: Check the fractional bandwidth: BW/f0 = 20 MHz ÷ 2000 MHz = 1%, and 1/QL = 0.01, so the two agree.

The coupling coefficient is g = Q0/Qe = 500/125 = 4, so the resonator is overcoupled: external loss dominates and QL (100) is well below Q0. Loosening the coupling raises Qe; at g = 1 (Qe = 500) QL would be 250 and the bandwidth 8 MHz.
examples.answer: QL = 100 and Qe = 125; g = 4, so the resonator is overcoupled.
examples.check:
f0 = 2e9
BW = 20e6
Q0 = 500.0
QL = f0/BW
Qe = 1.0/(1.0/QL - 1.0/Q0)
print(QL)
print(Qe)

examples.question: A copper (σ = 5.8×10⁷ S/m) air-filled cavity is made from the X-band guide of 1.7, a = 2.286 cm and b = 1.016 cm, closed by walls d = 2.0 cm apart. Find the TE101 resonant frequency, the unloaded Q and the unloaded bandwidth.
steps: Work in centimetres: kad = 2.087 × 2.286 × 2.0 = 9.542 cm, so (kad)³ = 868.9 cm³ and (kad)³bη = 868.9 × 1.016 × 376.7 = 3.325×10⁵ (cm⁴·Ω).
Unloaded bandwidth f0/Q0 = 9.965 GHz/7820 = 1.27 MHz. Critically coupled (Qe = Q0) the loaded Q is 3910 and the bandwidth 2.55 MHz.
examples.answer: f101 = 9.97 GHz, Q0 ≈ 7820 and an unloaded bandwidth of about 1.27 MHz (2.55 MHz when critically coupled).

traps: Using Q0 in QL = f0/BW when the resonator is connected. The measured bandwidth belongs to QL, not Q0.
Writing Q = BW/f0. Q is f0/BW, so wide bandwidth means low Q.
Calling a shorted λ/4 stub a series resonance. Its input impedance is infinite, so it is parallel; a shorted λ/2 line gives series resonance.
Forgetting Q0 and QL differ, and that loaded Q must be smaller than unloaded Q.
Mixing up the coupling words: Qe smaller than Q0 (g > 1) is overcoupled, not undercoupled; critical coupling is Qe = Q0, where QL = Q0/2.

quiz.q: Define the quality factor of a resonator in terms of stored energy and power loss.
quiz.a: Q = ω0 × (energy stored) ÷ (power lost), where ω0 = 2πf0 is the resonant angular frequency in rad/s. For a series circuit Q also equals ω0L/R.

quiz.q: Write the resonant frequency of an ideal LC resonator and name each symbol.
quiz.a: f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), with f0 in hertz, L in henries and C in farads.

quiz.q: Why does a high loaded Q mean a narrow bandwidth?
quiz.a: QL = f0/BW, so BW = f0/QL. For a fixed f0, raising QL shrinks the bandwidth. Physically, high Q means little energy is lost per cycle, so the resonance responds only over a small band around f0 and decays slowly in time.

quiz.q: A resonator resonates at 5 GHz with a loaded Q of 250. Find its 3 dB bandwidth. If its unloaded Q is 1000, find the external Q.
A rectangular cavity has a = 3 cm, b = 1.5 cm and d = 4 cm, air filled. Find the resonant frequency of the TE101 mode.
Using Zin = jZ0 tan(βl) for a shorted lossless line, explain why a shorted λ/4 stub acts as a parallel resonance and a shorted λ/2 line as a series resonance.
quiz.a: At l = λ/4, βl = π/2 and tan(βl) → ∞, so Zin → ∞: an open circuit, which is parallel resonance. At l = λ/2, βl = π and tan(βl) = 0, so Zin = 0: a short circuit, which is series resonance. The physical termination has not changed; only the electrical length has.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cavity filters in cellular base stations hold Q above 5000 and pass one channel, and acoustic-wave resonators set frequency in phone front ends. Superconducting cavities reach far higher Q in accelerators and quantum computing, where the stored-energy lifetime QL/ω0 must hold a qubit state. Search next for 'cavity perturbation measurement', 'Q measurement by ring-down' and 'coupling coefficient of a resonator'.
